hook.line: Hernando wants to know why Tomás was up at five. Was something pushing him, or was he aiming at something? Both answers end in a plain verb, and the tiny word before it carries the whole difference.
hook.es: Me levanté temprano para abrir el café.
hook.en: I got up early to open the café.

rule:
Both *por* and *para* can be followed by a plain *-r* verb. The meaning is opposite.

*Por* + verb looks back. It tells you the reason something happened: what caused it.
*Lo despidieron por llegar tarde.* Arriving late is what got him fired.

*Para* + verb looks forward. It tells you the goal: what someone is trying to achieve.
*Salimos temprano para no llegar tarde.* Arriving on time is what we are aiming at.

Quick test: if you could say *because he...*, use *por*. If you could say *in order to...*, use *para*.

English uses *for -ing* for the first and *to* for the second. Notice that Spanish gives you a different small word for each.
smallPrint: Teachers call this *por* (cause) against *para* (purpose) before an infinitive.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *por* or *para*: Lo despidieron ___ llegar tarde. (the cause)
yourTurn.why: Arriving late is the reason it happened: *por*.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *por* or *para*: Salimos temprano ___ no llegar tarde. (the goal)
yourTurn.answer: Salimos temprano para no llegar tarde.
yourTurn.why: It is what we are aiming at: *para*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: Vale went to the market to buy fruit.
yourTurn.answer: Vale fue al mercado para comprar fruta.
yourTurn.why: Buying fruit is her goal, so *para*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: Thank you for coming. (to a friend)
yourTurn.why: Coming is what you are thanking for: *por*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: They congratulated him for helping the neighbours.
yourTurn.answer: Lo felicitaron por ayudar a los vecinos.
yourTurn.why: Helping is the reason for the congratulations: *por*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: I study to talk with my grandmother.
yourTurn.answer: Estudio para hablar con mi abuela.
accept: Estudio para poder hablar con mi abuela.
yourTurn.why: Talking with her is the purpose: *para*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: He got up early to open the café. (Tomás)
yourTurn.answer: Tomás se levantó temprano para abrir el café.
accept: Se levantó temprano para abrir el café.
yourTurn.why: Opening the café is the purpose, so *para*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: Hablé en voz baja para despertar al bebé.
yourTurn.answer: Hablé en voz baja para no despertar al bebé.

pitfalls.why: Almost. Arriving late is the reason, not the goal, so *por*.

pitfalls.wrong: Salimos temprano por no llegar tarde.
pitfalls.right: Salimos temprano para no llegar tarde.
pitfalls.why: You are aiming at something, so use *para*.
After *gracias*, the reason you are thanking someone takes *por*.

pitfalls.wrong: Vale fue al mercado por comprar fruta.
pitfalls.right: Vale fue al mercado para comprar fruta.
pitfalls.why: Going to buy something is a purpose, so *para*.

personal: Say why you did something today with *por* and a verb, and what you did it for with *para* and a verb: *Salí temprano para...*
